newsitem.title: USA: AMR sees higher costs in 1997.
newsitem.headline: AMR sees higher costs in 1997.

text.p: AMR Corp, the parent of American Airlines, faces continued maintenance, labor and fuel cost pressures in 1997, AMR chief financial officer Gerard Arpey said.

While Arpey said American is "reasonably optimistic that 1997 will be a pretty good year," the airline's current labor dispute with its pilots union and fuel costs remain "wild cards" that could hinder the company's performance.

During a conference call with reporters, Arpey said "any work stoppage has dramatic adverse effects on our financial results, irrespective of how long it goes." Arpey declined to disclose the estimated costs of a possible strike.

The Allied Pilots Association last week rejected a tentative four-year contract with the airlines. AMR said it expected to go into a 30-day "cooling off" period since the pilots failed to meet the airline's deadline to accept binding arbitration from the National Mediation Board.
If no agreement is struck by the end of the "cooling off" period, the pilots would be free to strike. The airline could declare a lockout and implement new pay and work rules.
The labor uncertainties make it difficult for American to forecast its performance for 1997.

But the airline expects unit costs to increase about two percent in 1997 due to the higher costs to maintain its aging fleet, expanding labor expenses due to seniority pay increases and inflationary pressures, Arpey said.

In addition to rising "fixed costs," the airline also faces a $75 million bill to solve the so-called "year 2000" problem. The company will spend $30 million in 1997 to begin tackling the problem, Arpey said.
Despite the worries about costs, American expects strong traffic and bookings in the first quarter. Advanced bookings are up about two percent over last year, Arpey said.
American said its Dallas/Fort Worth and Chicago markets had solid fourth quarter performances, while the Hawaii market declined due to a "substantial increase" in capacity by competitors.

American also felt pressure on transcontinental routes due to the new Pan Am World Airways Inc, which returned to the skies in September. Internationally, American faces yield pressure in its Pacific markets.

Earlier on Wednesday, AMR posted fourth quarter profits of $284 million, or $3.08 a share, compared with a loss of $282 million, or $3.69 a share, in the fourth quarter of 1995. The 1996 fourth quarter included several extraordinary items.
The one-time charges included a $497 million gain on AMR's initial public offering of Sabre Group Holdings Inc, the company's reservations unit.
AMR said the gain was partly offset by a $230 million after-tax charge associated with the write-down of the company's investment in troubled Canadian Airlines.
Fourth quarter revenues rose 3 percent to $4.33 billion from $4.19 billion a year earlier.
AMR said it ended the year with a cash balance of $1.7 billion and $12 billion in total debt.
